concepts.alt: External secondary data are someone else's research you borrow or buy — handy, but tailored to their question, not yours.

terms.def: Data from outside the firm — census, trade journals, reports, websites, purchased research.
Data available for a fee from commercial research firms (e.g., Nielsen, Léger).

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Sephora uses industry sales reports and consumer trend data to plan assortments and promotions.

concepts.title: Disadvantages of secondary data
concepts.explain: Marketers must evaluate how secondary data were collected to ensure the information is reliable and relevant. Easy access to online data doesn't guarantee trustworthiness, especially when details about research design and sampling are unknown. Data mining of large digital sources also lets firms estimate metrics such as customer lifetime value (CLV) — the estimated long-term value of each customer to the firm.
concepts.alt: Secondary data is a second-hand car: check its history (how it was collected) before you trust it.

terms.def: A metric estimating the long-term value of each customer to the firm.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a blog statistic with no stated sample size or method shouldn't drive a major pricing decision.

concepts.title: Primary data — advantages & disadvantages
concepts.explain: Primary data are collected specifically to answer the current research question, using observation, surveys, interviews or focus groups. The main advantage: they can be tailored to the firm's specific decision needs. The disadvantages: they're typically more costly and time-consuming than secondary data. Proper design and unbiased collection are essential — poorly designed samples, biased questions or unrepresentative respondents lead to inaccurate conclusions.
concepts.alt: Primary data is a custom-tailored suit — fits perfectly, but costs more and takes longer than buying off the rack.

terms.def: Tailored to the firm's specific decision needs.
More costly and time-consuming than secondary data.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a phone maker runs its own survey of 2,000 Canadian students about camera features it's considering.

concepts.title: Qualitative (exploratory) research
concepts.explain: Qualitative research is exploratory — used to understand attitudes, perceptions and motivations rather than to measure them numerically. The slides list its methods as observation, social media, in-depth interviews, focus groups and projective techniques, and flag reliability, validity and sampling as considerations.
concepts.alt: Qualitative research asks "why?" and "how do you feel?" — it explores before quantitative research counts.

terms.def: Exploratory research aimed at understanding — via observation, social media, interviews, focus groups, projective techniques.

concepts.example: Illustrative: before designing a survey, a brand holds a few interviews to learn what words customers use to describe the product.

concepts.title: Observation research
concepts.explain: Observation research directly watches consumers' behaviours, in person or through cameras, sensors or eye-tracking. It's especially useful when consumers can't clearly explain their behaviour, revealing real usage patterns, shopping paths and product interactions. Observational and ethnographic insights help improve product design, store layouts, merchandising and promotions.
concepts.alt: Observation is "watch what they do, not what they say" — a heat map never lies about where shoppers walked.

terms.def: Directly watching consumers' behaviour, in person or via technology.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): in-store tracking systems and heat maps (Shopperception) show where shoppers look, move and interact with products.

concepts.title: Social media research
concepts.explain: Social media provide large volumes of real-time consumer opinions and behaviour. By monitoring and mining conversations, firms identify preferences, track brand sentiment and respond quickly to complaints or trends. Pros: large accessible sample, people of all ages, lots of brand-related data, very current, consumers freely offer opinions (no interviewer bias), data can be searched and filtered. Cons: not statistically representative, feedback may not be well thought out, anonymity can encourage extreme opinions, no depth about the consumer, no chance to probe, and no consent to study data (ethical issues).
concepts.alt: Social media is a giant, noisy town square — easy to overhear lots of honest opinions, but you can't ask follow-ups and the loudest voices aren't representative.

terms.def: Monitoring and mining social media conversations for insights.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a restaurant chain tracks negative mentions on X/TikTok in real time to respond to complaints.

concepts.title: In-depth interviews
concepts.explain: In-depth interviews are one-on-one conversations in which trained researchers ask detailed questions and probe further to understand respondents' experiences, attitudes and motivations. They provide rich individual-level insights but are time-consuming and relatively expensive, especially when specialised respondents are required.
concepts.alt: An in-depth interview is a deep conversation with one person — rich detail, but you can only have so many.

terms.def: A trained researcher asks detailed one-on-one questions and probes for deeper insight.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a medical-device firm interviews 12 surgeons individually about frustrations with current tools.

concepts.title: Focus groups
concepts.explain: A focus group brings together a small group of participants to discuss a specific topic under the guidance of a trained moderator, generating qualitative insights about attitudes and perceptions. It helps marketers understand reactions to products, advertising, pricing or competitors, often revealing insights surveys miss. Focus groups can now be run online, reducing costs and including participants from different locations.
concepts.alt: A focus group is a guided group chat — a moderator steers, participants spark off each other.

terms.def: A small group discussing a topic under a trained moderator to generate qualitative insights.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): A&W focus groups revealed many consumers thought a 1/4-pound burger was bigger than a 1/3-pound burger.

concepts.title: Projective techniques
concepts.explain: Projective techniques are named on the slides as one of the five qualitative research methods (alongside observation, social media, in-depth interviews and focus groups). The slides give no further definition, so for the midterm know it as a qualitative, exploratory method. (Flagged in CONTENT_NOTES — no definition invented.)
concepts.alt: Treat projective techniques as one of the "five qualitative tools" on the slide — recognise the name and its category.

terms.def: A qualitative research method listed on the slides (no definition provided).

concepts.example: Illustrative: on an exam, if asked which option is a qualitative method, 'projective techniques' is a valid answer per the slides.

concepts.title: Quantitative research
concepts.explain: Quantitative research uses numerical data to test hypotheses, measure relationships and support decisions. It can be descriptive (e.g., profiling brand users) or experimental (e.g., testing product formulations in controlled studies). Common methods: surveys, panel data collection and experiments.
concepts.alt: Quantitative research counts and tests — it turns opinions and behaviours into numbers you can compare.

terms.def: Research using numerical data to test hypotheses and measure relationships.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a survey of 1,000 shoppers measures how many prefer each of three package designs.

concepts.title: Surveys & questionnaire question types
concepts.explain: A survey is a quantitative method that collects information from respondents using a questionnaire designed to meet specific research objectives. Surveys can be administered online, by telephone, mail or in person. Questions may be unstructured (open-ended — respondents answer freely) or structured (closed-ended — predefined response options).
concepts.alt: Structured = multiple choice; unstructured = short answer.

terms.def: Collecting information from respondents using a questionnaire designed to meet research objectives.
Closed-ended, with predefined response options.
Open-ended, allowing respondents to answer freely.

concepts.example: Illustrative: 'Rate your visit 1–5' is structured; 'Tell us about your visit' is unstructured.

concepts.title: What to avoid when designing a questionnaire
concepts.explain: Avoid: questions respondents can't easily or accurately answer ("How much did you spend on groceries last month?"); sensitive questions unless necessary; double-barreled questions that refer to more than one issue with one set of responses; leading questions that steer respondents ("Volvo is the safest car on the road, right?"); one-sided questions that present only one side; questions with implicit assumptions ("Since caffeine is a stimulant, should children…"); and complex or unfamiliar questions ("Are mechanical watches better than quartz?").
concepts.alt: A good question is one question, neutral, answerable and plain — anything else bends the answers.

terms.def: Refers to more than one issue with only one set of responses.
Steers respondents to a particular response regardless of true beliefs.
Presumes the same point of reference for all respondents.
Presents only one side of an issue.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): 'Do you think Elizabeth May or Justin Trudeau would make a good prime minister?' is double-barreled.

concepts.title: Panel & scanner-based data
concepts.explain: Panel research collects ongoing purchase and behaviour data from the same group of consumers over time, tracking changes in preferences and responses to marketing. Scanner-based research captures real-time sales data at checkout from UPC codes, measuring how pricing, promotions and placement affect store sales. Both are often syndicated and together evaluate marketing strategies and improve product development.
concepts.alt: Scanner data is the receipt — what sold, when, where. Panel data is the diary — the same people tracked over time.

terms.def: Ongoing data from the same group of consumers over time.
Data from readings of UPC codes at checkout counters.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): the New Balance Tester Community panel gives ongoing feedback to refine sneakers.

concepts.title: Experimental research
concepts.explain: Experimental research manipulates one or more variables to determine their causal effect on outcomes such as sales, demand or profitability. Firms test pricing, advertising or product variations across test conditions and compare results to make evidence-based decisions.
concepts.alt: An experiment is an A/B test: change one thing, hold the rest steady, and see what it causes.

terms.def: Manipulating variables to determine their causal effect on outcomes.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): McDonald's tests different prices for a new combo across markets to find the most profitable price.

concepts.title: Marketing analytics & data warehouses
concepts.explain: Firms store massive amounts of customer and transaction information in data warehouses holding billions of data points. Marketing analytics uses advanced models and technologies to transform big data into insights that support better marketing decisions, integrating qualitative and quantitative methods to optimise marketing performance and customer strategies.
concepts.alt: The data warehouse is the library; analytics is the librarian who finds the useful book and reads you the key page.

terms.def: A store of massive amounts of customer and transaction data.
Using models and technology to turn big data into insights for marketing decisions.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a retailer's analytics team uses years of loyalty-card data to decide which stores get which products.

concepts.title: Descriptive, predictive, prescriptive & active analytics
concepts.explain: Descriptive analytics summarises past data; predictive analytics forecasts future outcomes; prescriptive analytics recommends optimal actions. Active analytics uses AI and Internet-of-Things data from connected devices to generate real-time insights. These tools help firms personalise offers, predict churn and improve decisions.
concepts.alt: Descriptive = "what happened?", predictive = "what will happen?", prescriptive = "what should we do?", active = "what's happening right now?"

terms.def: Summarises past data.
Forecasts future outcomes.
Recommends optimal actions.
Uses AI and IoT data for real-time insights.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Tesco analyses descriptive data on each product across 4,700 stores (up to 45 attributes) to target incentives to household profiles.

concepts.title: Marketing mix decisions made by analytics
concepts.explain: Marketing analytics helps firms make marketing mix decisions by analysing customer behaviour across multiple channels. Big data lets firms identify target segments and tailor assortments, promotions and communications to local markets. Loyalty programs and customer tracking provide purchase-pattern data used to personalise strategies.
concepts.alt: Analytics turns "what customers did" into "what we should sell, where, at what price and with which message".

terms.def: Analysing customer behaviour across many points of contact to guide the marketing mix.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): HSN gathers data across TV channels, catalogue and phone sales, and digital links.

concepts.title: Ethics of using customer information
concepts.explain: Ethical marketing research requires protecting consumer privacy, maintaining confidentiality and using data only for legitimate research purposes. Researchers must avoid misleading practices, misrepresenting results, or disguising selling as research. Laws and professional codes guide responsible collection, transparency and fair treatment. Smart devices can collect sensitive data (e.g., home layouts), so firms must obtain informed consent, disclose data use and protect data.
concepts.alt: Ethical research treats participants' data like a borrowed key — use it only for what you said, and never copy it for others.

terms.def: Participants agree to data collection knowing how it will be used.
Keeping participants' data private.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Frito-Lay's neuromarketing found shiny bags evoked guilt, so it switched to matte; a Roomba mapping and selling home layouts raises ethical concerns.

concepts.title: Product — the first P
concepts.explain: Product is the first P of the marketing mix and is essential to creating value for the consumer. Products include not only physical goods and services but also places, ideas, organisations, people and communities that create value through exchange. New products range from minor improvements and new flavours to breakthrough innovations. Product strategy focuses on innovation, new product development, market adoption and managing products through their life cycle.
concepts.alt: "Product" is anything someone would exchange value for — a shampoo, a city to visit, a cause to support, even a celebrity.

terms.def: Anything — good, service, place, idea, organisation, person — that creates value through exchange.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): the Bartesian prototype shows a novel concept (a cocktail machine) becoming a tangible offering.

concepts.title: Why firms create new products
concepts.explain: Innovation is the process of transforming ideas into new products and services that help firms grow and stay competitive. Firms innovate because customers get bored and preferences change — standing still loses money. New products vary along a continuum of newness, from new-to-the-world innovations to redesigned or improved versions of existing products. Despite high failure rates, firms innovate for long-term value, new revenue streams and growth. Reasons covered: changing customer needs, market saturation, managing risk through diversity, fashion cycles and improving business relationships.
concepts.alt: Without innovation a firm is stuck selling the same thing to the same people — and they'll eventually get bored.

terms.def: The process by which ideas are transformed into new products and services that help the firm grow.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): the Amazon Echo was new-to-the-world; Toronto Kayaks' clear LED boats are innovative design, not a breakthrough.

concepts.title: Changing customer needs
concepts.explain: New products create value by meeting changing customer needs or preventing boredom with existing offerings. Innovation can come from breakthrough ideas, redesigning existing products, aging markets or legislation (which can be opportunities or threats). Firms that anticipate unrecognised needs or regulatory shifts can shape entire markets.
concepts.alt: Customers' needs are a moving target; the winners aim where it's going, not where it was.

terms.def: Shifts in needs/wants that new products can satisfy.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Dyson redesigned the century-old vacuum so it doesn't lose suction.

concepts.title: Market saturation
concepts.explain: As markets mature, there are many competitors and growth slows — market saturation. Saturation makes continuous innovation essential. Firms can find growth in niche markets and dietary trends (e.g., gluten-free) and can diversify their product portfolios to manage risk and stabilise performance.
concepts.alt: A saturated market is a full parking lot; to grow you need a new lot (niche) or a new kind of car (innovation).

terms.def: A market with many competitors where growth has slowed.
Offering varied products to manage risk and stabilise performance.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): General Mills reformulated and labelled Chex as gluten-free to capture health-conscious and celiac consumers.

concepts.title: Fashion cycles
concepts.explain: Industries with short product life cycles — fashion, apparel, entertainment, gaming, software — depend heavily on continuous new product introductions. Most revenues in entertainment and software come shortly after release, and consumer demand for novelty drives repeat purchases. Apparel designers produce entirely new selections a few times a year.
concepts.alt: In fashion, the product's shelf life is a season — so the new collection is always already in the works.

terms.def: Short product life cycles driven by demand for novelty, requiring frequent new introductions.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Zara relies on continuous new product introductions.

concepts.title: Improving business relationships
concepts.explain: New products can strengthen supplier relationships, not just target end consumers. Retailers use supplier data to identify unmet demand and co-develop new offerings. Even successful innovations spread gradually through diffusion.
concepts.alt: New products can be a team project between a retailer and its suppliers — sharing data to spot gaps both can fill.

terms.def: Using new products and shared data to strengthen supplier/retailer partnerships.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Walmart asks suppliers for data on all products they sell, not only those sold at Walmart, to find unmet demand.

concepts.title: Diffusion (adoption) of innovation
concepts.explain: Diffusion of innovation is the process by which the use of an innovation spreads throughout a market group over time and across categories of adopters. Adoption happens at different rates across consumer groups. The theory helps marketers understand the rate at which consumers are likely to adopt a new product, forecast demand, identify target markets, and design promotion and pricing for each group. The number of users over time generally follows a bell-shaped curve.
concepts.alt: Diffusion is like a new song spreading: a few fans find it first, then their friends, then the radio, then your parents.

terms.def: The process by which the use of an innovation spreads through a market over time and across adopter categories.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): new Call of Duty versions sell fast early, while others wait for reviews, price drops or peer recommendations.

concepts.title: Pioneers, first-mover advantage & disruptive innovation
concepts.explain: Pioneers (breakthroughs) are new-to-the-world products that create new markets or radically alter existing ones. Being first brings first-mover advantage: strong brand recognition and early market share, and research shows pioneers can keep larger shares longer than later entrants. Disruptive innovations are simpler, lower-cost alternatives that change industries.
concepts.alt: A pioneer clears a new trail; whoever walks it first gets their name on the map.

terms.def: New-to-the-world products that create new markets or radically alter existing ones.
Benefits of being first — brand recognition and early market share.
A simpler, lower-cost alternative that changes an industry.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Apple's iPod sparked an accessory ecosystem; Netflix disrupted video rental, contributing to Blockbuster's decline.

concepts.title: Pioneer challenges & why new products fail
concepts.explain: Not all pioneers succeed: followers (copycats) can improve on early weaknesses, and pioneers pave the way for new entrants. As many as 95% of new consumer goods fail. The main cause is failing to assess the market properly (poor testing, wrong target, poor positioning). Other causes: too few benefits, too much complexity or learning, bad timing, and brand misalignment (venturing beyond the firm's competencies or image).
concepts.alt: Being first is a head start, not a guarantee — the second runner can draft behind you and sprint past.

terms.def: As many as 95% of new consumer goods fail.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Google Glass failed over privacy concerns, bugs and public bans; Vine paved the way for TikTok.

concepts.title: Adopter categories
concepts.explain: Purchasers are divided into five groups by how soon they adopt: innovators (first 2.5%, risk-takers, not price sensitive), early adopters (13.5%, wait for reviews but still buy early and influence others), early majority (34%, want bugs resolved; drive profitability — a product must "cross the chasm" to reach them), late majority (34%, adopt once the product is established, often price sensitive), and laggards (16%, resist change and may never adopt). Innovators and early adopters generate early momentum and word-of-mouth.
concepts.alt: Picture a phone launch: innovators camp overnight, early adopters buy after a few reviews, the early majority waits for bugs to be fixed, the late majority buys last year's model, and laggards keep the flip phone.

terms.def: First 2.5% — risk-takers who love newness.
Next 13.5% — wait for reviews but buy early and influence others.
34% — adopt once risks are reduced; drive profitability.
34% — adopt after the product is established.
16% — resist change; may never adopt.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): innovators line up overnight for a new iPhone; laggards still use flip phones.

concepts.title: Diffusion factor — relative advantage
concepts.explain: The speed of diffusion depends on product characteristics: relative advantage, compatibility, observability, complexity and trialability. Relative advantage: if a product is perceived to be better than substitutes, diffusion is relatively quick. Clear functional benefits make adoption easier and faster, and advertising can demonstrate value across user situations.
concepts.alt: Relative advantage answers "Why switch?" — the clearer the upgrade, the faster people jump.

terms.def: The degree to which a product is perceived as better than substitutes.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): the Swiffer makes cleaning faster and easier, especially for seniors; the telephone replaced the telegraph by transmitting voices.

concepts.title: Diffusion factor — compatibility
concepts.explain: Compatibility: when an innovation aligns with existing values, lifestyles and behaviours, diffusion accelerates; when it conflicts, it slows. Cultural differences influence diffusion speed, so firms adapt product features to fit regional needs.
concepts.alt: Compatibility asks "Does it fit how I already live?" — a product that slots into habits spreads faster.

terms.def: The degree to which an innovation fits consumers' existing values, lifestyles and behaviours.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Starbucks expanded quickly in coffee-loving Canada but more slowly in tea-dominant China and Japan; Swiffer must be smaller for Japanese homes.

concepts.title: Diffusion factor — observability
concepts.explain: Observability: when people see others using and loving a product, it serves as social proof. Visible, shareable benefits accelerate diffusion; demonstrations and viral content reduce uncertainty. Low observability can slow diffusion, especially for personal-use products.
concepts.alt: Observability is "seeing is believing" — if everyone can see it working, more people try it.

terms.def: The degree to which a product's benefits are visible to others.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Blendtec's 'Will It Blend?' videos blended iPads and baseballs, going viral and boosting awareness.

concepts.title: Diffusion factors — complexity & trialability
concepts.explain: Complexity is how hard an innovation is to understand, learn or use; lower complexity speeds diffusion. Trialability is the degree to which an innovation can be experimented with; easier trial reduces uncertainty and increases adoption (free trials, returns, in-store demos). Less complex products are usually easier to try, so they diffuse faster.
concepts.alt: Simple + easy to test-drive = fast adoption. Confusing + no way to try = slow adoption.

terms.def: How hard an innovation is to understand, learn or use.
The degree to which an innovation can be experimented with before committing.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Dyson's interactive in-store displays let shoppers try the vacuum and see dirt pickup; a 30-day free trial of software.

concepts.title: The new product development process
concepts.explain: The new product development (NPD) process has six steps: idea generation (developing viable ideas), concept testing (testing the idea among potential customers), product development (developing prototypes and the product), market testing (testing the actual product in a few test markets), product launch (full-scale commercialisation), and evaluation of results (analysing performance and making modifications). Diagrams show it as sequential, but in reality it is iterative and cross-functional; teams revisit earlier steps, and firms sometimes skip stages for speed or cost — which increases risk.
concepts.alt: NPD is "idea → test the idea → build it → test the product → launch → check how it did", with plenty of loops back.

terms.def: Idea generation → concept testing → product development → market testing → product launch → evaluation of results.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a snack firm brainstorms a flavour, surveys reactions to a description, makes test batches, sells them in one city, launches nationally, then tracks sales and reviews.

concepts.title: Idea source — internal R&D & reverse innovation
concepts.explain: Idea sources include internal R&D, licensing, brainstorming, outsourcing, competitors' products and customer input. Many firms — especially large ones that can afford it — rely on internal R&D; heavy investment can accelerate breakthrough innovation, and a strong innovation culture supports long-term development. Reverse innovation is when products are developed for consumers in developing economies and later introduced into developed countries.
concepts.alt: Internal R&D is a firm's own idea lab; reverse innovation is when that lab's best ideas come from emerging markets first.

terms.def: A firm's own research and development used to generate new product ideas.
Products developed for developing economies, later introduced into developed countries.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): an ECG machine built cheaply for rural clinics in India later used in U.S. ambulances; Fujitsu's business tablets.

concepts.title: Idea source — licensing
concepts.explain: Firms can acquire innovation through licensing instead of internal R&D: they buy the right to use technology or ideas from another (research-intensive) firm through a licensing agreement. Licensing reduces development costs and gives access to cutting-edge technology, but depends on external expertise and banks on a solution that already exists but hasn't been marketed.
concepts.alt: Licensing is renting someone else's invention instead of building your own from scratch.

terms.def: Buying the right to use technology or ideas from another firm through a licensing agreement.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Qualcomm licenses its 5G technology to Apple; small biotech firms license inventions to large pharma.

concepts.title: Idea source — brainstorming
concepts.explain: Brainstorming encourages free idea generation without immediate criticism; ideas are evaluated only after the creative phase ends. Entrepreneurial pivots often emerge from structured idea generation, and environmental forces can influence the ideas.
concepts.alt: Brainstorming has one rule: no judging until the idea pile is done.

terms.def: Generating ideas freely without immediate criticism; evaluation comes later.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): during COVID-19, an aerospace machine shop brainstormed a pivot to Henson Shaving precision safety razors.

concepts.title: Idea source — outsourcing
concepts.explain: Firms outsource innovation when internal capabilities are limited — lacking resources or expertise. Specialised firms bring fresh perspectives; cross-disciplinary teams (anthropologists, engineers, designers, psychologists) enhance creativity and user-centred design, and external collaboration can significantly increase firm value.
concepts.alt: Outsourcing innovation is hiring a specialist chef when your own kitchen can't make the dish.

terms.def: Hiring external specialist firms to generate or develop new product ideas.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): SimpliSafe hired IDEO to redesign all 15 system components, leading to a video doorbell and a $1 billion valuation.

concepts.title: Idea source — competitors' products & reverse engineering
concepts.explain: A competitor's successful launch may signal unmet demand or new technical possibilities. Firms analyse rival offerings through reverse engineering — taking apart a competitor's product, analysing it and creating an improved product that doesn't infringe patents. Copycat strategies are common across consumer and technology markets; reverse-engineered products must be substantively different from the source.
concepts.alt: Reverse engineering is studying a rival's recipe by tasting the dish — then cooking a better, legally different version.

terms.def: Taking apart and analysing a competitor's product to create an improved, non-infringing product.

concepts.example: Illustrative: after a rival's wireless earbuds sell well, a firm disassembles them to design longer-lasting batteries.

concepts.title: Idea source — customer input & lead users
concepts.explain: Customer input is essential for idea generation in B2B and B2C markets. Observation and social media reveal expressed and unexpressed needs. Lead users — innovative customers aware of emerging trends — help firms anticipate them, especially in fashion. In B2B markets, firms often work closely with a few customers for frequent feedback and joint development, which increases the likelihood the customer adopts the product.
concepts.alt: Lead users are the customers who are already living in the future — watch what they do and you'll see what's next.

terms.def: Innovative product users who modify products themselves and are aware of emerging trends.
Ideas from customers via feedback, observation, social media and co-development.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): fashion designers change designs based on trends spotted on the street; healthcare firms co-design with patients.

concepts.title: Concept testing
concepts.explain: Promising ideas are developed into concepts — brief written and/or visual descriptions of the product, its features, technology, working principles and the need it satisfies. Concept testing presents the concept to potential buyers to gauge their reaction and, most importantly, their purchase intention. It uses marketing research techniques (surveys, interviews). Early testing reduces risk and prevents costly development mistakes; concepts that respondents don't like never move on.
concepts.alt: Concept testing is pitching the idea before building it — "Would you buy this if it existed?"

terms.def: A brief written/visual description of a product idea, its features and the need it satisfies.
Presenting the concept to potential buyers to gauge reactions and purchase intentions.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a start-up shows students a one-page description and sketch of a reusable smart water bottle and asks whether they'd buy it.

concepts.title: Product development — prototypes, alpha & beta testing
concepts.explain: In product development an engineering team builds a prototype — the first physical form of the new product — based on concept testing findings, deciding materials, dimensions and specifications. Prototypes are tested in two ways. Alpha testing: internal teams test whether the product performs according to its design and satisfies the need (internal vetting). Beta testing: potential customers examine the prototype in a real-use setting to assess functionality, performance and problems.
concepts.alt: Alpha = "we test it in-house". Beta = "real customers test it in real life".

terms.def: The first physical form of a new product.
Internal testing to check the product performs according to design.
Potential customers test the prototype in a real-use setting.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Ben & Jerry's alpha tests flavours with employees; Bartesian went through prototypes P1–P5.

concepts.title: Market testing — premarket tests vs test marketing
concepts.explain: Market testing takes two forms. Premarket tests expose the product to potential customers in a controlled environment (often run by research firms like ACNielsen) to estimate how many will try and keep using it — generating a sales estimate so the firm can decide to introduce or modify the product. Test marketing releases the product in a limited geographic area before national launch; it involves actual production and distribution and can prevent larger losses, but it reveals the product to competitors.
concepts.alt: Premarket test = a dress rehearsal in a controlled room. Test marketing = opening night in one small town before the national tour.

terms.def: Exposing potential customers to a product in a controlled setting to estimate trial and repeat use.
Introducing the product in a limited geographic area before the national launch.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Ben & Jerry's sampling a new flavour at Costco; a product launched in one part of a city before a national rollout.

concepts.title: Product launch
concepts.explain: If market testing is positive, the firm launches the product to the entire market — full-scale commercialisation. Launch involves confirming the target market, deciding the positioning, and finalising the marketing mix, including the first-year budget. The right product must hit the market at the right time and price, and a launch without sufficient resources can fail no matter how good the product is.
concepts.alt: Launch is opening day — the product can be great, but without the right timing, price and budget, nobody shows up.

terms.def: Full-scale commercialisation: confirming target market, positioning and marketing mix.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a phone maker coordinates a global release date, pricing, ads and retail stock for launch week.

concepts.title: Evaluation of results
concepts.explain: After launch, marketers conduct a critical post-launch review to determine whether the product and its launch succeeded, and what resources or marketing-mix changes are needed. They look at quality, functionality, durability, customer satisfaction and KPIs (sales, reviews, ratings, ROI). Understanding why a product fails is as important as why another succeeds; an underperforming product may need further development.
concepts.alt: Evaluation is the post-game review: what worked, what didn't, and what to change before the next play.

terms.def: Post-launch analysis of performance (KPIs, satisfaction) and needed modifications.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a snack brand tracks first-quarter sales, reviews and repeat purchases, then tweaks the flavour.

concepts.title: Product life cycle stages
concepts.explain: The product life cycle (PLC) defines the stages a product moves through: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Introduction: low sales and high costs, negative or low profits (initial losses), innovators, one or few competitors. Growth: rising sales as acceptance grows, rapidly rising profits, early adopters and early majority, few but increasing competitors. Maturity: sales peak and growth slows as the market saturates, profits peak then decline, late majority, many competitors. Decline: falling sales and shrinking margins, laggards, few competitors — firms may discontinue, find new uses or innovate.
concepts.alt: The PLC is a product's biography: birth (intro), adolescence (growth), middle age (maturity), retirement (decline).

terms.def: Stages a product moves through: introduction, growth, maturity, decline.
Low sales, high costs, initial losses; innovators buy.
Rising sales and profits; early adopters and early majority.
Sales peak, market saturates, many competitors; late majority.
Falling sales and profits; laggards; few competitors.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): EVs are in growth with increasing competitors; many consumer packaged goods are in maturity.

concepts.title: Strategies for extending the PLC
concepts.explain: In maturity, firms can extend the life cycle by: developing new uses, modifying the product (quality, performance, packaging), increasing frequency of use, increasing the number of users, finding new users, repositioning the product, and tweaking the marketing strategy.
concepts.alt: When a product plateaus, give it a new job, a makeover, more reasons to use it, or new people to use it.

terms.def: New uses, modify product, increase frequency, increase users, find new users, reposition, tweak strategy.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Apple cuts prices on older models to reach new segments; Arm & Hammer promotes baking soda in many rooms; Campbell's publishes recipes using soup.

concepts.title: PLC curve variations & caveats
concepts.explain: The PLC curve is theoretically bell-shaped, but real markets vary. The slides show high-learning products (slow, long introduction), low-learning products (rapid early growth), fashion products (repeating cycles) and fad products (rapid rise and fall). The PLC is useful but must be applied cautiously: it is hard to know which stage a product is in, and misreading it (e.g., treating a product as declining) can create a self-fulfilling decline. Data-driven iteration helps avoid premature withdrawal.
concepts.alt: The PLC is a map, not GPS — if you misread where you are and cut support, you can drive the product into decline yourself.

terms.def: Needs a long introduction while customers learn about it.
Easy to understand; sales take off quickly.
Sales rise and fall in repeating cycles.
Rapid rise and quick fall.
Misdiagnosing a product as declining, then withdrawing support so it does decline.

concepts.example: Illustrative: a viral toy that sells out for one holiday season and then disappears follows a fad curve.

concepts.title: Complexity of products — core, actual, augmented
concepts.explain: Products have layers. Core customer value is the basic problem-solving benefit consumers seek. Marketers translate it into the actual product — brand name, packaging, quality level, features and design. Associated services (augmented product) add long-term value: financing, product warranty and product support.
concepts.alt: Think of an onion: the core is the benefit you want, the next layer is the physical thing you buy, and the outer layer is the service wrapped around it.

terms.def: The basic problem-solving benefits consumers seek.
Brand name, packaging, quality level, features and design.
Financing, warranty and product support that add value.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Trek's Madone 9 bike — core value of fast riding, actual product with carbon frame and shifting, plus custom fit options.

concepts.title: Types of consumer products
concepts.explain: The slides classify consumer products into four types, illustrated by example: specialty (e.g., a medical professional — a specialty service), shopping (e.g., apparel), convenience (e.g., soft drinks), and unsought (e.g., insurance — an unsought service). The slides don't give longer definitions, so learn the types through these examples.
concepts.alt: Convenience = grab it (pop). Shopping = compare it (clothes). Specialty = seek out a specific one (a particular doctor). Unsought = don't think about it until you must (insurance).

terms.def: Example from slides: soft drinks.
Example from slides: apparel.
Example from slides: a medical professional.
Example from slides: insurance.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): soft drinks (convenience), apparel (shopping), a medical professional (specialty), insurance (unsought).

concepts.title: Product mix & product lines
concepts.explain: The product mix is the complete set of all products offered by a firm. Product lines are groups of associated items, such as those consumers use together or think of as part of a group of similar products. Colgate-Palmolive's mix includes oral care, personal care, home care and pet nutrition lines.
concepts.alt: The product mix is the whole store; product lines are the aisles.

terms.def: The complete set of all products offered by a firm.
A group of associated items consumers use together or see as similar.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Colgate-Palmolive — Oral Care (Colgate Total), Personal Care (Speed Stick, Irish Spring), Home Care (Palmolive, Ajax), Pet Nutrition (Hill's Science Diet).

concepts.title: Product category
concepts.explain: A product category is an assortment of items that customers see as reasonable substitutes for one another.
concepts.alt: A product category is the "either one would do" group — like different toothpastes.

terms.def: An assortment of items customers see as reasonable substitutes for one another.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): within Colgate's oral care line, toothpaste is a category (e.g., Colgate Total) and whitening products another.

concepts.title: Product mix breadth & product line depth
concepts.explain: Breadth (variety) is the number of product lines a firm offers. Depth is the number of products within a product line. Firms can increase breadth by adding new product lines or decrease it by deleting entire lines; they can similarly add or cut products within a line to change depth.
concepts.alt: Breadth = how many aisles; depth = how many items on each aisle's shelves.

terms.def: The number of product lines offered by a firm.
The number of products within a product line.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Colgate's four lines (oral, personal, home, pet) show breadth; the many toothpaste and brush products in oral care show depth.

concepts.title: Brands & brand elements
concepts.explain: A brand consists of the terms, designs, symbols or other features that identify one seller's good or service as distinct from others'. Brand elements include: brand name (the spoken component — descriptive, unrelated or invented, e.g., Comfort Inn, Apple, Accenture), URLs/domain names, logos and symbols (symbols are logos without words — the Nike swoosh, the Mercedes star), characters (Pillsbury Doughboy; Snap, Crackle and Pop), slogans (State Farm's "Like a Good Neighbour", Tim Hortons' "Always Fresh"), jingles (Intel's four-note signature), and even distinctive packages.
concepts.alt: Brand elements are the brand's "ID kit" — name, face (logo), mascot, catchphrase and theme song.

terms.def: Terms, designs, symbols or features that identify one seller's product as distinct from others'.
The spoken component of branding.
A logo without words.
A short phrase describing or persuading about the brand.
An audio message of words or distinctive music.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Under Armour's slogan 'The Only Way Is Through' featuring Tom Brady.

concepts.title: Value of branding
concepts.explain: Branding creates value in six ways: brands facilitate purchasing, establish loyalty, protect from competition, reduce marketing costs, are assets, and impact market value. The purpose of branding is to help consumers distinguish one company's products from another's.
concepts.alt: A strong brand is a shortcut for customers and a shield and a bank account for the firm.

terms.def: Facilitates purchasing, establishes loyalty, protects from competition, reduces marketing costs, is an asset, impacts market value.

concepts.example: Illustrative: shoppers quickly grab a familiar brand on a crowded shelf — the brand facilitates purchasing.

concepts.title: Brand equity (branding framework)
concepts.explain: The branding framework has three parts: brand equity (brand awareness, perceived value, brand associations, brand loyalty), brand ownership strategies (manufacturer brand, store/private label, generic), and brand name strategies (family brand, individual brand). Brand equity is the set of assets built through these four components.
concepts.alt: Brand equity is the brand's "credit score" — built from how well-known it is, how worth-it it seems, what it reminds people of and how loyal they are.

terms.def: Brand awareness, perceived value, brand associations, brand loyalty.

concepts.example: Illustrative: Apple's equity rests on high awareness, perceived value, strong associations and loyal customers.

concepts.title: Brand awareness
concepts.explain: Brand awareness measures how many consumers in a market are familiar with the brand, know what it stands for and have an opinion about it. Some brands are so strong they've become synonymous with the product itself.
concepts.alt: Awareness is name recognition — the strongest brands become the everyday word for the product.

terms.def: How many consumers are familiar with the brand and what it stands for, and have an opinion of it.

concepts.example: Illustrative: people say 'Kleenex' for tissue or 'Google it' for searching online.

concepts.title: Perceived value
concepts.explain: Perceived value is the relationship between a product's benefits and its costs, often compared with competing products. Value depends on balancing benefits and cost; value-focused brands succeed by aligning quality expectations with price. Private-label brands have grown because consumers believe they offer similar quality to national brands at lower prices.
concepts.alt: Perceived value is the "worth it?" meter — benefits on one side, cost on the other.

terms.def: The relationship between a product or service's benefits and its costs.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Apple's premium prices are justified for many by design, innovation, ecosystem and reliability; supermarket private labels offer similar quality for less.

concepts.title: Brand associations, intimacy & personality
concepts.explain: Brand associations are the mental links consumers make between a brand and attributes, emotions and meanings. Brand intimacy reflects deep emotional bonds between consumers and brands, and brand personality gives brands human-like characteristics. Associations go beyond awareness into identity and feeling.
concepts.alt: Associations are what pops into your head when you hear the brand — and how you feel about it.

terms.def: Mental links consumers make between a brand and attributes, emotions and meanings.
Deep emotional bonds between consumers and brands.
Human-like characteristics attributed to a brand.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Starbucks tops fast-food brand-intimacy studies; Tesla built intense emotional connections around innovation.

concepts.title: Brand loyalty
concepts.explain: Brand loyalty brings several benefits: loyal consumers are often less sensitive to price, marketing costs are much lower, loyal customers praise their favourite products and retailers, and a high level of loyalty insulates the firm from competition.
concepts.alt: Loyal customers are a brand's fan club — they pay a bit more, cost less to keep, and recruit their friends.

terms.def: Commitment to repurchase a brand; reduces price sensitivity and marketing costs and insulates from competition.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Dove rewarded loyal consumers with double PC Optimum points at Shoppers Drug Mart.

concepts.title: Brand ownership — manufacturer, private-label, generic
concepts.explain: Brand ownership strategies: manufacturer brands are owned and managed by the manufacturer (e.g., Cherry Coke); private-label (store) brands are owned and managed by retailers (e.g., President's Choice Black Cherry); and generics carry no brand name beyond the product description (e.g., "Cherry Cola").
concepts.alt: Who owns the name? The maker (manufacturer), the store (private label), or nobody (generic).

terms.def: A brand owned and managed by the manufacturer.
A brand owned and managed by a retailer.
An unbranded product sold by its product description.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Cherry Coke (manufacturer), President's Choice Black Cherry (private label), plain 'Cherry Cola' (generic).

concepts.title: Family vs individual brands
concepts.explain: Brand name strategies: a family brand uses a combination of the company brand name and an individual brand name to distinguish products, with several product lines sold under one name (e.g., Kellogg's, Kraft). Individual brands use a separate brand name for each product (e.g., Tide; Kraft's Velveeta, Classico, Jell-O, Grey Poupon). A firm can use both.
concepts.alt: Family brand = everyone shares the family surname. Individual brand = each kid gets their own name with no surname on show.

terms.def: Uses the company brand name (with individual names) across products.
Separate brand names for each of a firm's products.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Kellogg's (family brand) vs Tide (individual brand); Kraft uses both.

concepts.title: Choosing a brand name
concepts.explain: A good brand name should be descriptive and suggestive of the product's benefits and qualities; easy to pronounce, recognise and remember; registered as a trademark and legally protected; and easy to translate.
concepts.alt: Good names are like good usernames: say what you're about, easy to say and remember, actually yours, and work in other languages.

terms.def: Descriptive/suggestive, easy to pronounce/recognise/remember, trademark-protected, easy to translate.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): discussion question — is Tostitos a good brand name? What about Lay's?

concepts.title: Brand extension — benefits
concepts.explain: A brand extension uses the same brand name for new products. Benefits: a well-established name, perceived high quality carries over, lower marketing costs, synergy among complementary products, and a boost to sales of the core brand.
concepts.alt: Brand extension borrows the reputation you've already built — a new product starts with a famous last name.

terms.def: Using the same brand name for new products.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Ferrari licenses its name to apparel for fans who can't afford the car; Starbucks selling branded mugs and tumblers.

concepts.title: Brand extension risks & avoiding brand dilution
concepts.explain: Brand extensions can backfire. Too many extensions lead to brand dilution; the core brand and extension may not fit well; and brand associations may not be similar. To avoid dilution: evaluate the fit between the core brand's product class and the extension; evaluate consumer perceptions of the core brand's attributes and seek extensions with similar attributes; refrain from extending the name to too many products; and make sure the extension can be distanced from the core brand if needed.
concepts.alt: Stretch a rubber band too far, or in a weird direction, and it snaps — that's brand dilution.

terms.def: Weakening of brand equity when the name is extended too far or to poorly fitting products.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Zippo's women's perfume failed (people don't link lighters with perfume); Kate Spade Saturday stores closed within two years.

concepts.title: Cobranding
concepts.explain: Cobranding markets two or more brands together on one product or promotion. Partnerships can enhance perceived quality and expand target segments, but misaligned customer bases or conflicts can lead to failure.
concepts.alt: Cobranding is a duet — two brands perform together to reach both fan bases.

terms.def: Marketing two or more brands together on one product or promotion.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Yum! Brands combines KFC and Taco Bell in one location; the GoPro–Red Bull partnership aligns two action-oriented brands.

concepts.title: Brand licensing
concepts.explain: Brand licensing is a contractual agreement in which a licensor grants a licensee the right to use its brand name, logo, symbols or characters in exchange for royalties (lump-sum or percentage of sales). It generates royalty revenue and increases brand visibility, but overexposure or misuse can dilute brand equity. It's common in apparel, toys, entertainment and video games.
concepts.alt: Brand licensing is renting out your brand — someone else makes the product, you collect rent (royalties).

terms.def: A licensor lets a licensee use its brand for a fee (royalties).
The brand owner / the firm paying to use the brand.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Disney licenses Mickey Mouse to partners for toys and apparel (e.g., Herschel).

concepts.title: Packaging
concepts.explain: Packaging attracts attention and differentiates brands, communicates promotions and product benefits, and different sizes target different retail channels and segments. Packaging can drive rebranding, accessibility and sales growth.
concepts.alt: Packaging is the product's outfit and its billboard — it gets noticed, tells you what's inside, and can make the product easier to use.

terms.def: The container/wrapping that attracts attention, differentiates, communicates and can add functional value.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): Degree Inclusive by Unilever — easy-grip shape, magnetic closures and one-handed application for people with upper-limb disabilities.

concepts.title: Labelling
concepts.explain: Labels provide essential product and regulatory information. Canadian laws require accuracy, bilingual content and transparency. Labels are also powerful promotional tools, and nutritional and benefit claims influence perceived value.
concepts.alt: A label is both a legal ID card (what's required to say) and a mini ad (what you want to brag about).

terms.def: Providing product and regulatory information on packaging; also a promotional tool.

concepts.example: Illustrative (from slides): siggi's highlights '18g protein' per serving on the front of the package to signal health benefits.

shortAnswers.q: Explain the macroenvironmental factors (CDSTEP) that influence a firm's marketing strategy and provide an example of each.
shortAnswers.model:
Macroenvironmental factors are broad external forces summarised as CDSTEP. Culture is the shared meanings, beliefs, values and customs of a group; firms must consider both country culture (Canada vs. Japan) and regional subcultures (Ontario vs. Quebec) — for example, Quebec residents are less likely to buy hot prepared meals. Demographics are characteristics of populations such as generational cohorts, income, education, gender and ethnicity; Harley-Davidson's Tough Turban for Sikh riders responds to Canada's changing ethnic composition. Social trends include greener consumers, privacy concerns, a time-poor society, food waste and health and wellness — Patagonia's refurbished clothing appeals to green consumers.

Technological advances create new products, communication methods and retail channels; AI, robotics and the Internet of Things let firms like Stitch Fix personalise offerings. The economic situation — inflation, interest rates, exchange rates and recession — affects spending; a weak Canadian dollar attracts tourists to Canadian retailers, while recessions push consumers toward essentials. Finally, the political/legal environment includes laws such as the Competition Act and labelling rules, which can restrict marketers but also create opportunities, such as demand for child car seats. Firms monitor all six factors proactively and adjust their marketing mix.
mistakes: Including microenvironment factors (competition, partners) as CDSTEP.
Defining 'S' as 'suppliers' instead of social trends.
Naming factors without examples.

shortAnswers.q: A new bubble-tea shop is opening near McMaster. Explain how its microenvironment would influence its marketing strategy.
shortAnswers.model:
The microenvironment consists of factors close to the firm that directly affect its ability to serve customers: company capabilities, competition and corporate partners, with the consumer at the centre of the framework. First, the shop should assess its company capabilities and core competencies — for example, its recipe know-how, staff, location and finances — and focus on customer needs that match them, such as fast, customisable drinks for students between classes.

Second, it must analyse competition. Direct competitors are other bubble-tea shops near campus, while indirect competitors (Tim Hortons, Starbucks, energy drinks) compete for the same share of the student's wallet. Using competitive intelligence — visiting rivals, tracking their prices and promotions on social media, reading reviews — the shop can improve where competitors fail, such as offering faster mobile ordering. Third, it depends on corporate partners: tapioca and milk suppliers, delivery apps and possibly the university for campus events. Strong partner relationships create a seamless system so drinks are available when and where students want them. Together these factors shape its product, price, place and promotion decisions.
mistakes: Writing about CDSTEP macro factors instead of the microenvironment.
Omitting indirect competitors.
Not applying factors to the bubble-tea shop.

shortAnswers.q: Inflation and interest rates are high and a recession is possible. Explain how these economic conditions could affect a mid-priced restaurant chain and how it might respond.
shortAnswers.model:
The economic situation is a macroenvironmental factor that affects how consumers buy and spend. Inflation is the general rate of price increases; when it stays above the roughly 2% target, it erodes purchasing power, so customers seek lower prices and better value. High interest rates raise the cost of borrowing, and with household debt already high, consumers cut discretionary purchases such as eating out. A recession — negative economic growth for at least two consecutive quarters — shifts spending toward essentials and low-cost luxuries.

For a mid-priced restaurant chain, this could mean fewer visits and smaller orders, particularly among value-conscious middle-class families whose purchasing power has been squeezed. The chain could respond by emphasising value: introducing smaller-portion or set-price menus, loyalty rewards, and positioning a meal out as an affordable "low-cost luxury". It could also monitor exchange rates, since a weaker dollar may raise imported ingredient costs but bring in more tourists. Being proactive rather than reactive lets it adjust its marketing mix before sales fall.

rubric.point: Inflation erodes purchasing power / value seeking
Interest rates = cost of borrowing; reduce discretionary spending

mistakes: Confusing interest rates with exchange rates.
Defining recession vaguely as 'a bad economy'.
No specific response for the restaurant.

shortAnswers.q: List and briefly explain the social and natural trends that impact marketing decisions.
shortAnswers.model:
Social and natural trends shape consumer values, change over time and can be opportunities or threats. Greener consumers want environmentally friendly products — 69% say they'd pay a premium — so firms use green marketing, while stricter laws require proof of claims to prevent greenwashing. Privacy concerns are growing: 80% of people want more control over their data, and tracking backlash (like the Tim Hortons app) and costly breaches mean firms must protect and explain how they use data.

A time-poor society spends more time working, so consumers multitask and value services that save time, such as cleaning, errands and meal delivery. Efficient food distribution reflects food trends (organic, portion control, calorie apps) and efforts to reduce food waste through AI, apps and donation programs. Health and wellness concerns fuel a large wellness industry — fitness apps, yoga, wellness services — while regulators push responsible food marketing to children. These trends are also connected to the UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals.
mistakes: Listing CDSTEP factors instead of the specific social trends.
Forgetting to explain each trend's marketing implication.

shortAnswers.q: Explain the five steps of the consumer decision process. Provide an example for each step.
shortAnswers.model:
The consumer decision process describes the steps consumers go through before, during and after a purchase. It begins with need recognition, when a consumer notices a gap between their current state and a desired state — for example, a student realises their laptop's battery can't last through a day of classes. Needs can be functional (performance) or psychological (status, self-image). Next is information search: the student uses internal search (remembering how their last brand performed) and external search (asking friends, reading reviews). Search effort increases with cost and perceived risk. In alternative evaluation, the student compares a small evoked set of brands on evaluative criteria such as price, battery life and weight, possibly using a compensatory rule or a shortcut such as "known brands are safer".

In the purchase decision step, intentions must be converted into a purchase; retailers reduce friction with easy checkout, multiple payment options and fast delivery so the student doesn't abandon the cart. Finally, in postpurchase, the student evaluates the purchase. The outcome can be satisfaction, postpurchase dissonance (buyer's remorse, more likely with an expensive item) or loyalty. Marketers support satisfaction by building realistic expectations, demonstrating correct use, offering warranties, encouraging feedback and following up with customers.

rubric.point: Need recognition — gap between current and desired state (functional/psychological)
Alternative evaluation — evoked set / evaluative criteria / decision rules
Purchase decision — converting intention; reducing friction

mistakes: Listing the steps without explaining what happens in each.
Putting alternative evaluation before information search.
Forgetting postpurchase — the process doesn't end at the purchase.
Using one generic example instead of tying an example to each step.

shortAnswers.q: Maya is usually a careful, budget-conscious shopper. Explain how the three situational factors could lead her to buy an expensive item she didn't plan to buy. Use course concepts.
shortAnswers.model:
Situational factors are factors specific to the situation that can override, or at least influence, a consumer's psychological and social tendencies. Even though Maya is normally budget-conscious, the purchase situation could change her choice: if she is buying a gift for her best friend's graduation, the occasion may make a premium brand feel more appropriate than her usual discount option. The shopping (sensory) situation also matters — soft lighting, elegant displays, pleasant music, aroma and attentive sales staff can make products feel more luxurious and encourage her to buy something she hadn't planned.

Finally, her temporal state — time pressure and mood — can push her to act. If the graduation is tomorrow and a sale ends today, she may buy immediately rather than keep shopping around. Mood matters too: a stressful day could make her spend more or less than usual. Together these three factors explain why Maya's actual purchase can differ from her normal careful behaviour, which is why retailers invest in store atmosphere, occasion-based promotions and time-limited offers.

rubric.point: Defines situational factors as overriding/influencing psychological & social factors
Purchase situation — occasion such as a gift

mistakes: Confusing situational factors with psychological factors like lifestyle or attitudes.
Naming the three factors without applying them to Maya.
Calling the store environment the 'purchase situation'.

shortAnswers.q: Explain the psychological factors that influence the consumer decision process and provide examples.
shortAnswers.model:
Psychological factors are influences internal to the consumer: motives, attitudes, perception, learning and lifestyle. A motive is a need or want strong enough to drive action; Maslow's hierarchy describes physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualization needs — a Subway ad, for example, appeals to the physiological need for food. An attitude is a learned, lasting evaluation with cognitive (beliefs), affective (feelings) and behavioural (actions) components, such as believing yoga is healthy, feeling calm about it and enrolling in classes.

Perception is how we select, organise and interpret information through our senses; consumers filter messages through selective exposure, attention, comprehension and retention, so marketers design packaging and stores that stand out (e.g., a café's warm lighting and aroma create a premium feel). Learning is a change in thought or behaviour from experience — a positive trial of Tide's Eco-Box can build a repeat-purchase habit. Lifestyle reflects how people spend time and money and how they want to live; a Tiffany purchase may signal a milestone, status-oriented lifestyle. Together these factors shape each step from need recognition to postpurchase.

rubric.point: Defines psychological factors as internal to the consumer

mistakes: Mixing in social factors (family, reference groups) as psychological.
Listing factors without definitions or examples.
Writing 'psychological needs' (from need recognition) instead of psychological factors.

shortAnswers.q: A new athletic-wear brand wants to sell to first-year university students. Explain how social factors could influence these students' purchases and how the brand could use them.
shortAnswers.model:
Social factors include family, reference groups and culture. For first-year students, reference groups are especially powerful. Their membership groups — their residence floor, program or varsity team — act as benchmarks for what to wear, so the brand could sponsor intramural teams or residence events. Aspirational groups, such as varsity athletes or fitness influencers they admire, could be used in campaigns to make the brand desirable, while the brand should avoid associations with dissociative groups that students want to distance themselves from. Reference groups influence buying by sharing information, rewarding approved behaviour and shaping self-image, which creates social proof.

Family still matters: parents may act as influencers or even decision makers if they pay, so messaging could address both students (style) and parents (value and durability). Culture also shapes values and shopping behaviour; the brand should show it genuinely understands the diverse cultural backgrounds of students — for example, offering inclusive sizing or modest athletic options — rather than making superficial gestures. Using these social factors lets the brand build adoption among a group that strongly looks to peers for cues.

rubric.point: Identifies social factors: family, reference groups, culture
Concrete brand actions applied to students

mistakes: Describing psychological factors (attitudes, motives) instead of social factors.
Mixing up aspirational and dissociative groups.
No specific recommendations for the brand.

shortAnswers.q: Compare how a consumer would make the decision to buy a new car versus a carton of milk. Use the concepts of involvement, perceived risk and types of buying decisions.
shortAnswers.model:
Involvement is how much a consumer cares about a purchase. A car is a high-involvement purchase because it is expensive, risky, infrequent and often expressive of identity. It carries significant perceived risk: financial risk (a large monetary outlay plus operating costs), performance risk (the car may be unreliable), physiological risk (safety), and social and psychological risk (how others see the car and how the buyer feels about it). As a result, the buyer engages in extended problem solving: researching reviews, visiting dealers, comparing options on many attributes and perhaps using a compensatory rule. Under the elaboration likelihood model, they would process car ads deeply.

Milk is a low-involvement, low-risk, frequently bought item. The consumer uses habitual decision making, automatically repurchasing a familiar brand with almost no conscious effort, or at most limited problem solving if their usual brand is out of stock. They spend almost no time searching and would process milk ads superficially. Marketers therefore provide detailed information, test drives and warranties for cars, but focus on shelf presence, availability and reminders for milk.

rubric.point: Defines involvement; car = high, milk = low
Perceived risk types for the car

mistakes: Calling milk 'impulse buying' — it's planned and routine, i.e., habitual.
Not naming specific risk types.
Describing the products without the course terms.

shortAnswers.q: Elizabeth is creating a new product focused on educating school children. Explain how Elizabeth should position her product. Be sure to back up your answers with what you have learned in this course.
shortAnswers.model:
Positioning is the mental picture — the thoughts, feelings and impressions — that customers have of a product relative to competing products. Before positioning, Elizabeth should complete the earlier STP steps: segment the market (for example demographically by children's age, and by parents' benefits sought such as academic results or fun) and target an attractive segment that is identifiable, reachable, responsive and substantial. Because children use the product but parents and teachers often buy it, she should position to the decision makers as well as the users. To choose a position, she can build a perceptual map: determine how parents perceive existing educational products (e.g., on "fun vs. academic" and "affordable vs. premium"), identify competitors' positions, determine consumer preferences, select an open position, and monitor it over time.

She could then use one or more positioning methods. Product-attribute positioning would stress the features most important to her target, such as curriculum alignment or adaptive learning. Benefits & symbolism positioning would emphasise the benefit (confident, curious kids) and a friendly character or symbol children recognise. Value positioning would highlight strong learning outcomes relative to price, and competition positioning could compare her product with screen-only games ("all the fun of a game, with real learning"). Her marketing mix — design, packaging, price and distribution through schools — should consistently communicate the chosen position.

rubric.point: Defines positioning (mental picture relative to competitors)
Links to segmentation and targeting first
Recognises parents/teachers as buyers and children as users
Applies at least two positioning methods
Consistent marketing mix supports the position

mistakes: Describing segmentation only and never stating a position.
Listing positioning methods without applying them to Elizabeth's product.
Claiming market-leadership positioning for a brand-new product with no share.
Ignoring that parents/teachers make the purchase decision.
